prompt.context: Our client is a pharmaceutical company with two divisions. Each division has a separate sales force. Division I manufactures a diagnostic test (like a blood sugar test) and Division II manufactures a pill or drug or treatment (say, Claritin).
prompt.question: Does it make sense for the divisions to combine the sales forces into a single sales force?

clarifying_info.q: How large is each sales force?
clarifying_info.a: Division I requires a sales force of 75 people. Division II requires a sales force of 50 people.

clarifying_info.q: Are the sales people equally skilled/effective?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Each sales person is equally effective at selling and makes a standard frequency of hospital visits each month to hospitals in their respective regions.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two sales forces target the same doctors or hospital contacts?
clarifying_info.a: No. The doctors and health professionals targeted by the two sales forces are in totally separate parts of the hospitals and do not come into contact with one another.

framework: Frame the decision around profitability impact: does combining the sales forces increase overall profitability?
Revenue impact: assess whether combining increases sales volume (do the two forces serve the same or different customers/doctors?)
Cost impact: one-time implementation costs (retraining, severance, reorganization) vs. ongoing synergies (smaller combined headcount serving the same doctors)
Expertise/relationship risk: evaluate whether generalist reps lose the specialist credibility that drives physician trust
Net recommendation: weigh cost savings against revenue risk given the customer overlap finding

questions.prompt: What is the potential revenue impact of combining the sales forces?
questions.guidance: Strong answers note that revenue upside from combining depends on customer overlap. Since the two sales forces target completely different doctors in separate parts of the hospital, there is little opportunity for a rep to make a single visit that sells both products. Revenue could actually fall if specialization is lost: doctors view sales reps as trusted expert advisors, and a generalist rep may be perceived as less credible. Also flagging relationship disruption if some reps are made redundant.

questions.prompt: What is the potential cost impact of combining the sales forces?
questions.guidance: Strong answers distinguish one-time costs from ongoing savings. One-time costs: retraining all remaining reps on both product lines, severance for any reps laid off, reorganization costs. Ongoing savings: if the combined force can cover the same number of doctors with fewer total reps, the firm saves on salaries, benefits, travel, and management overhead. Current total sales force = 75 + 50 = 125 people; the relevant question is whether the combined force needs fewer than 125 reps to maintain the same coverage given separate doctor targets.

math.setup: Current combined headcount: 75 (Div I) + 50 (Div II) = 125 reps. If doctors are in different hospital areas and still need separate visits, a combined rep must make the same number of visits as two separate reps, implying no headcount reduction is possible without reducing coverage.
steps: Div I reps: 75; Div II reps: 50; total: 125
If each combined rep still needs to make two separate visits (to two different doctor groups), total visit load does not change, so the required headcount stays at 125
No headcount savings are achievable under the given facts
math.answer: Under the given assumptions (separate doctor targets, equal visit frequency required), there are no headcount savings. One-time costs are incurred with no ongoing offset.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional factors or risks should be considered when deciding whether to combine the sales forces?

categories.name: Revenue risks
ideas: Loss of specialist expertise and doctor trust if reps become generalists
Relationship disruption when existing reps are reassigned or let go
Different selling cycles or complexity for diagnostics vs. drugs may disadvantage a generalist rep
Potential conflict of interest if the two products compete for the same physician attention or formulary slot

categories.name: Cost considerations
ideas: Retraining costs for all retained reps on the other division's product
Severance costs for any reps made redundant
Possible reduction in travel costs if visits happen to be at the same hospital (though still separate departments)

categories.name: Organizational factors
ideas: Different incentive structures may be needed for diagnostic vs. pharmaceutical sales
Management complexity of overseeing a combined force with two product lines
Cultural integration challenges between two previously separate teams

categories.name: Strategic fit
ideas: Whether the combined sales model aligns with long-term product portfolio strategy
Whether competitors in both segments use combined or separate forces
Whether the firm plans to launch additional products that would benefit from a combined force

recommendation: Based on the available facts, combining the sales forces does NOT appear to increase profitability
The two forces target completely different doctors in separate hospital areas, eliminating the primary source of revenue synergy (consolidated visits)
There are real one-time costs (retraining, severance, reorganization) with no clear offsetting headcount savings or revenue uplift
risks: Revenue may fall if specialist credibility is lost with physicians who rely on reps as trusted experts
Relationship capital built by existing reps could be destroyed if those reps are reassigned or let go
next_steps: Conduct a detailed analysis of actual visit patterns to confirm there is truly no customer overlap
Model the full cost of retraining and any severance to quantify the one-time cost burden
Explore whether keeping the forces separate but sharing back-office or administrative resources could capture some savings without the revenue risk
